books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A: More than four million Americans crossed the Appalachian Mountains between 1800 and 1840 to settle in the West. Many Southern planters moved into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, and later Texas, hoping to recreate the Cotton Kingdom, complete with slave labor, on cheaper land. Farmers from the upper South moved into southern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, while New England and New York families settled in northern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, as well as Wisconsin and Michigan. Over time, the towns and churches of the Old Northwest began to resemble New England, while the plantations of the newly settled South resembled the Old South. Meanwhile, most immigrants who arrived between 1800 and 1860 came from northern and western Europe. Four-fifths of Irish immigrants settled in port cities of the Northeast, while German immigrants, often with more money, moved on to the “German triangle” of Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A. Paraphrased, not quoted.

stem: The pattern of westward settlement described in the passage shows that migrants

options.text: settled wherever land was free, with no regard for where they came from
options.misconception: The passage shows the opposite: settlers carried their home regions' ways with them.

options.text: carried the ways of their home regions with them
refused to bring slavery into the new western lands
options.misconception: Southern planters brought enslaved labor west to recreate the Cotton Kingdom.

options.text: settled mainly in cities along the Atlantic coast
options.misconception: The passage is about crossing the Appalachians into the West, not about staying on the coast.

rationales.A: The passage sorts migrants by origin: upper South to southern Ohio, New England to the north. Origin shaped where they settled.
rationales.B: The passage ends with the pattern: Old Northwest towns and churches resembled New England, while the new Southern settlements resembled the Old South. Migrants rebuilt the world they knew.
rationales.C: Planters carried slavery west on purpose, hoping to recreate the Cotton Kingdom on cheaper land.
rationales.D: The migrants crossed the Appalachians into the West. The Atlantic coast is where they started, not where they settled.
rationales.general:
1. Sort the migrants by origin. Upper South families went south of the line, New England families went north.
2. Read the last sentence. The Old Northwest resembled New England; the new South resembled the Old South.
3. Name the pattern. Migrants carried their home regions west with them.
Background: New communities grew quickly, with migrants depending on one another to clear land, build dwellings, and create a sense of community.
Remember: a settlement pattern is a map of where people came from.
